title: errors.Is, errors.As, errors.Join; sentinels vs error types
summary: Sentinels answer "which failure?", error types carry data, and errors.Is, errors.As and errors.AsType find either anywhere in a wrapped tree. Whatever you wrap with %w becomes your API, so translate driver errors at the boundary.

examples.title: Sentinels with errors.Is, error types with errors.AsType and errors.As

annotations.note: A sentinel is matched by identity, so its message text plays no part. Exporting one makes it API: callers will depend on it. io.EOF and sql.ErrNoRows are the standard library's best-known sentinels.
An error type carries fields the caller can act on. Error has a pointer receiver, so *ValidationError is the error type, and it is the type to ask for below.
== compares only the outermost value, the wrapper fmt.Errorf built on line 23. errors.Is walks the chain, comparing each link with == or asking the link's own Is method.
A type assertion has the same blind spot as ==: it sees only the outer wrapper, so one more layer of context breaks it. Never type-assert errors you didn't just create.
errors.AsType (Go 1.26) returns the first *ValidationError in the chain, already typed. errors.AsType[ValidationError] wouldn't compile: the value type has no Error method.
errors.As does the same through a pointer to a target variable; code written before Go 1.26 uses it. Passing verr instead of &verr panics at run time, and go vet's errorsas check reports it.

examples.title: errors.Join and several %w build a tree that Is and As search

annotations.note: Limits on names and places should count characters. len counts UTF-8 bytes: "Şanlıurfa" is 9 runes but 11 bytes, and a byte limit of 10 would reject a valid Turkish city.
Collect, then join once. errors.Join drops nil values and returns nil when nothing is left, so the valid path (line 40) needs no special case.
A joined error prints one line per error, which suits logs. An API that returns a list of field errors can get the parts through the Unwrap() []error method that Join's result implements.
Is and As search the whole tree depth-first, so each check finds its error whichever branch holds it.
Since Go 1.20 fmt.Errorf accepts several %w, and the result unwraps to all of them. errors.Unwrap only follows Unwrap() error, so it returns nil here: inspect with Is and As, never by hand.

examples.title: Translating a driver error at the repository boundary

annotations.note: A stand-in so the example needs no database. The real type is pgx's *pgconn.PgError, and SQLSTATE 23505 is unique_violation in PostgreSQL's error code table.
%w passes the driver type through, so callers can, and will, write errors.AsType[*pgconn.PgError]. Your service now depends on pgx, and changing the storage breaks code that never touched SQL.
The translation: %w on ErrEmailTaken, %v on the driver error. The message keeps the SQLSTATE and constraint name for the log; the only link callers can inspect is the sentinel you chose to promise.
Other driver errors stay opaque too: the caller logs them and answers 500. If callers must detect something from below, such as context.Canceled, wrap that one on purpose.
The same text, a different API: errors.Is succeeds only on the translated error, and only the leaky one exposes the driver type.

use_cases: Sentinels for conditions callers branch on: ErrNotFound, ErrEmailTaken, io.EOF, sql.ErrNoRows
Error types when callers need data: the field that failed validation, a retry-after duration, an HTTP status from an upstream API
errors.Join for form validation that reports every field at once, and for cleanup that fails after the main operation failed
Translating pgx or HTTP-client errors into domain errors inside the repository or client package
strengths: Matching is by identity or type, never by message text, so messages can change (or be localized) without breaking callers, unlike parsing exception messages
errors.Is and errors.As walk any depth of wrapping, so each layer can add context without breaking inspection further up
Exposure is an explicit choice at each call site: %w makes the cause inspectable, %v keeps only its text, and the message reads the same either way
errors.AsType is checked at compile time: asking for a type that doesn't implement error fails to build instead of panicking
weaknesses: Nothing tells the caller which sentinels and types a function can return; it lives in doc comments, unlike Java's throws clause
Every exported sentinel and error type is API surface you have to keep
Trees from errors.Join and several %w have no single cause: errors.Unwrap returns nil, and order of the search matters when two links match

pitfalls.title: Comparing with == or asserting the type
pitfalls.detail: err == ErrNotFound and err.(*MyErr) both fail as soon as any layer wraps the error. Use errors.Is and errors.AsType (errors.As before Go 1.26).

pitfalls.title: Matching on err.Error() text
pitfalls.detail: Messages are not API, and OS text differs by platform and language: on Windows, Go asks for the English message and falls back to the system language when it isn't available. Match sentinels and types instead.

pitfalls.title: Passing a non-pointer to errors.As
pitfalls.detail: errors.As(err, verr) panics at run time; it needs &verr. go vet's errorsas check catches it, and errors.AsType makes the mistake impossible.

pitfalls.title: Wrapping driver errors with %w out of habit
pitfalls.detail: Callers start depending on *pgconn.PgError and SQLSTATE codes. Translate to your own sentinel with %w and keep the driver error as %v text.

quiz.q: err := fmt.Errorf("load: %w", ErrNotFound). What does err == ErrNotFound return?
quiz.why: err is the wrapper fmt.Errorf created; only errors.Is looks inside it.

quiz.q: When is an error type better than a sentinel?
options: When the caller needs data about the failure, such as which field
When the error is returned from many places
quiz.why: A sentinel only identifies the failure; a type carries fields the caller can use.

quiz.q: err := errors.Join(errA, errB). What does errors.Unwrap(err) return?
quiz.why: errors.Unwrap only calls Unwrap() error; Join's result has Unwrap() []error, which Is and As use instead.

quiz.q: Your repository gets a *pgconn.PgError with code 23505. What should it return?
quiz.why: Callers get an inspectable domain sentinel and the full text for logs, without depending on the driver's type.

further_reading.title: The Go Blog: Working with Errors in Go 1.13 (Whether to wrap)
Go 1.20 Release Notes: wrapping multiple errors

body:
## Concept

There are two ways to make an error something callers can inspect. A sentinel is a
package-level value, `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`, checked with
`errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)`. It answers "which failure was it?". An error type is a
struct with an `Error` method, checked with `errors.AsType[*ValidationError](err)` (Go
1.26) or `errors.As(err, &target)`. It answers "which failure, and with what details?".

Both functions search the chain `%w` builds, and since Go 1.20 that chain can be a tree:
`errors.Join` and `fmt.Errorf` with several `%w` produce errors with several children,
searched depth-first. A type can also customize matching with an `Is(error) bool` method.
That is why the previous lesson's `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` worked on Linux and
Windows alike: `syscall.Errno` has an `Is` method that maps each OS's own "file not
found" codes to `fs.ErrNotExist`.

The design rule comes from the Go blog: wrapping with `%w` makes the wrapped error part
of your API. Wrap what you are willing to support; format the rest with `%v`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `catch (ValidationException e)` looks only at the thrown exception;
  `errors.AsType[*ValidationError](err)` is that catch plus a walk down `getCause()`.
  `errors.Is` is the same walk looking for one specific instance. `errors.Join` plays
  the role of suppressed exceptions, but as an ordinary value.
- Python: `except ValidationError as e:` maps to `AsType`, `raise DomainError() from e`
  to `%w`, and `ExceptionGroup` (3.11) to `errors.Join`.
- JS/TS: `err instanceof ValidationError` plus `err.cause` (ES2022) is the same search
  done by hand; `AggregateError` corresponds to `errors.Join`.
- C: errno values are sentinels without a chain, and `strerror` text was never meant to be
  matched either.

## Design notes

Prefer, in this order: opaque errors (the caller only checks `err != nil`), then sentinels
for the few conditions callers really branch on, then error types when they need data.
Every exported sentinel and type is a promise, so add them when a caller needs one, not
in advance. Translate at package boundaries: the repository turns `*pgconn.PgError` with
SQLSTATE 23505 into `ErrEmailTaken`, the HTTP layer turns `ErrEmailTaken` into 409, and
neither knows the other's vocabulary. The next lesson puts that mapping in one place and
adds the panics that slip past it. Never match on `err.Error()` text: on Windows, Go
asks the OS for English messages and falls back to the system language, so the same
failure can read differently on different machines.

  err == ErrNotFound: false
  errors.Is:          true

  type assertion: false
  errors.AsType:  id / must be positive
  errors.As:      id / must be positive

name: required
city: 13 characters, max 10
required? true
too long: city 13
valid: true

true true <nil>

create user: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_email_key" (SQLSTATE 23505)
